title: Generating and Evaluating Tests for K-12 Students with Language Model Simulations: A Case Study on Sentence Reading Efficiency
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to efficiently generate and calibrate parallel literacy assessment forms for K-12 students, focusing on silent sentence reading efficiency. The authors argue that traditional test development is expensive and slow because experts must write items and then collect large amounts of student response data to calibrate difficulty and reliability. Their core question is whether large language models can help automate item generation and calibration while still producing tests that function similarly to expert-written forms.

The intervention is not a classroom learning tool but an AI-supported assessment-development pipeline. GPT-4 was used to generate true/false sentence items designed to be readable by young children, and a separate fine-tuned language model was trained as an item-response simulator using prior student response data. This simulator predicted how past students would respond to unseen items, including both accuracy and response time, allowing the researchers to estimate item ambiguity and difficulty. The authors then used these simulated parameters to assemble AI-generated parallel test forms intended to match an existing human-developed Sentence Reading Efficiency (SRE) test.

The study used several populations and contexts. The training dataset included 1,962 participants ranging from 1st grade through high school and adulthood, drawn from more than 30 diverse school partners in the United States over two school years. Evaluation also included 50 Prolific crowdworkers and a real-world school deployment with 234 students in grades 2-8 from a California public school, of whom 231 were retained after excluding likely random guessers. The school-based task was administered online/self-administered as timed test blocks comparing a human-generated form with an AI-generated form that had been additionally reviewed by humans for safety and ambiguity.

The main conclusion is that the AI-assisted pipeline can produce sentence reading efficiency test forms that closely resemble expert-developed forms in score patterns and difficulty. In the school evaluation, total scores on the AI-generated and human-generated forms were highly correlated (r = 0.93), and in crowdworker testing the parallel AI form also closely matched the lab form (r = 0.92). The item-response simulator outperformed a traditional readability metric (Flesch-Kincaid) for predicting item response time and difficulty. However, the authors also emphasize that human review remained necessary, that generalizability beyond this specific reading-efficiency task is unproven, and that demographic and deployment differences may limit transfer.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 case study with real student data and clear methods, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of a learning intervention. The main evidence is correlational/comparative test-form validation, so it fits yellow rather than green or blue.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows promising but indirect impact: strong equivalence between AI- and human-generated assessment forms (r=0.93), but no direct evidence of improved student literacy outcomes. Impact is therefore meaningful for assessment operations yet unclear for learner outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI is used to generate and calibrate parallel sentence-reading-efficiency assessment items and test forms for K-12 students, with a fine-tuned LLM simulating student responses to estimate item difficulty, ambiguity, and response time.

finding.finding_summary: In a school evaluation with 234 students in grades 2-8 (231 analyzed after exclusions), scores on the AI-generated sentence reading efficiency test were highly correlated with scores on the human-generated test form (r=0.93). This indicates the generated test form closely matched the standard form in reading-efficiency measurement, but the study evaluates assessment equivalence rather than improvement in student literacy learning or comprehension gains.
finding.measure: Sentence Reading Efficiency (SRE) total scores; correlation between AI-generated and human-generated test forms; item-level predicted vs actual response time and accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that LLM-supported item generation can reduce the burden of constructing parallel reading assessments by producing test forms that align closely with expert-developed forms. In the K-12 school study (n=234), the AI-generated form produced highly correlated scores with the lab form (r=0.93), supporting feasibility for more scalable assessment development, though direct teacher-time or cost savings were not quantified.
finding.measure: Assessment form equivalence/reliability; scalability of item generation and calibration via simulated student responses
finding.study_size: n=234 students; training dataset n=1962 participants with 183,782 responses

finding.finding_summary: The study provides initial K-12 deployment evidence that LLM-generated parallel reading-efficiency tests can function similarly to expert-written forms in a real school context, which may support institutional progress-monitoring capacity. However, the evidence is limited to one case study and does not directly measure district-, school-, or policy-level outcomes.
finding.measure: School-deployed parallel test-form comparability for progress monitoring
